reminder: A path integral adds up the weight $e^{iS/\hbar}$ over all histories of a system, where $S$ is the action.
definition: A path integral gives a number for a physical system by integrating the weight $e^{iS[\phi]/\hbar}$ over the space of all histories $\phi$ of the system. Here $S$ is the [action functional](c:action-functional) of the system, and the path integral is a model of [quantization](c:quantization). In the Euclidean version the weight is $e^{-S[\phi]/\hbar}$, and a [measure](c:measure) can make the integral rigorous.
examples: Particle on a line: the [integral kernel](c:integral-kernel) of time evolution from $a$ to $b$ is the sum of $e^{iS[x]/\hbar}$ over all paths $x$ from $a$ to $b$.
Euclidean case: the Feynman-Kac formula writes $e^{-tH}$, with $H=-\tfrac12\Delta+V$, as an integral of $e^{-\int_0^t V(x_s)\,ds}$ over paths $x$ with respect to [Wiener measure](c:wiener-measure).
Finite model: $\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}e^{-S(x)/\hbar}\,dx$ is the path integral of a system with $n$ degrees of freedom and no time.
Non-example: the symbol $\mathcal{D}x$ in the real-time formula is not a Lebesgue measure, because no translation-invariant measure exists on an infinite-dimensional space of paths.

reminder: Every algebraic extension of a perfect field is separable.
definition: A [field](c:field) $F$ is perfect if every [algebraic extension](c:algebraic-extension) of $F$ is [separable](c:is-separable). Equivalently, $F$ has [characteristic](c:characteristic) $0$, or it has characteristic $p>0$ and the [Frobenius map](c:frobenius) $x\mapsto x^p$ is onto $F$.
examples: The rational numbers and every other field of characteristic $0$ are perfect.
Every finite field and every algebraically closed field is perfect.
Non-example: the field $\mathbb{F}_p(t)$ of rational functions is not perfect, because $t$ has no $p$-th root and $x^p-t$ is irreducible but inseparable.

steps: Take a [field](c:field) $F$.
Add the condition that every algebraic extension of $F$ is separable.
A field with this condition is perfect.
links.why: It shows that perfect is a condition on a field, and that every field of characteristic $0$ meets it.

steps: Take a field $F$ of [characteristic zero](c:char-zero) and an irreducible polynomial $f$ over $F$.
The derivative $f'$ is nonzero and has smaller degree, so $f$ and $f'$ have no common factor.
So $f$ has no repeated root, and every algebraic extension of $F$ is separable.
links.why: It shows why characteristic $0$ is enough for a field to be perfect.

steps: Take a [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$ of characteristic $p$.
The Frobenius map $x\mapsto x^p$ is injective on a finite set, so it is onto.
A field of characteristic $p$ with onto Frobenius map has no irreducible polynomial that is inseparable.
So every algebraic extension of $\mathbb{F}_q$ is separable.
links.why: It shows that the finite fields are the standard perfect fields of positive characteristic.

reminder: Two lines are perpendicular when they meet at a right angle.
definition: Two [lines](c:line) that meet are perpendicular if the [angle](c:angle) between them is $90^\circ$. In $\mathbb{R}^n$ this means that their direction vectors $u$ and $v$ satisfy $u\cdot v=0$.
examples: The $x$-axis and the $y$-axis of the plane are perpendicular.
The lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with directions $(1,2)$ and $(2,-1)$ are perpendicular, because $1\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)=0$.
Non-example: the lines $y=0$ and $y=x$ meet at an angle of $45^\circ$, so they are not perpendicular.

steps: Give $\mathbb{R}^n$ its dot product as inner product.
Two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is $0$.
Call two lines through one point perpendicular when their direction vectors are orthogonal.
links.why: It shows that perpendicular is orthogonality for the direction vectors of lines in Euclidean space.

reminder: A $\pi$-system is a family of sets that is closed under finite intersections.
definition: A $\pi$-system on a [set](c:set) $X$ is a family $\mathcal{P}$ of subsets of $X$ such that $A\cap B\in\mathcal{P}$ whenever $A\in\mathcal{P}$ and $B\in\mathcal{P}$. That is, $\mathcal{P}$ is closed under the [intersection](c:intersection) of two members.
examples: The half-lines $(-\infty,a]$ with $a\in\mathbb{R}$ form a $\pi$-system, because $(-\infty,a]\cap(-\infty,b]=(-\infty,\min(a,b)]$.
The measurable rectangles $A\times B$ form a $\pi$-system on a product $X\times Y$.
Every [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) is a $\pi$-system, and so is every topology.
Non-example: the family $\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$ is not a $\pi$-system, because $\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ is missing.

steps: Take a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{A}$ on $X$.
It is closed under countable intersections, so it is closed under the intersection of two members.
So $\mathcal{A}$ is a $\pi$-system, and the converse fails because a $\pi$-system need not contain complements.
links.why: It shows that a sigma-algebra is a $\pi$-system with more closure properties.

reminder: A positive linear functional is a linear map to the scalars that never takes a negative value on a positive element.
definition: Let $V$ be a [vector space](c:vector-space) with a notion of [positive elements](c:positive-element), such as an ordered vector space or a [C*-algebra](c:c-star-algebra). A [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $\varphi$ on $V$ is positive if $\varphi(x)$ is a real number with $\varphi(x)\ge0$ for every positive $x$.
examples: Integration $f\mapsto\int f\,d\mu$ on the continuous functions with compact support is positive for every measure $\mu$.
Evaluation $f\mapsto f(x_0)$ at a point is a positive linear functional on the continuous functions on a space.
The trace on the matrices $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ is positive, because $\operatorname{tr}(a^*a)=\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2\ge0$.
Non-example: $f\mapsto f'(0)$ on $C^1([-1,1])$ is linear but not positive, because $f(x)=(x-1)^2\ge0$ has $f'(0)=-2$.

steps: Take a linear functional $\varphi$ on an ordered vector space.
Add the condition that $\varphi(x)\ge0$ whenever $x\ge0$.
Then $\varphi$ is monotone: $x\le y$ implies $\varphi(x)\le\varphi(y)$, by linearity.
links.why: It shows that positivity is one order condition on top of linearity, and that it gives monotonicity.

steps: A [positive linear map](c:positive-linear-map) sends positive elements of one ordered space to positive elements of another.
Take $\mathbb{C}$ with its usual order as the target.
The positive elements of $\mathbb{C}$ are the numbers $\ge0$, so the map is a positive linear functional.
links.why: It shows that a positive functional is a positive map whose target is the scalar field.

reminder: A Hermitian matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite when $x^*Ax\ge0$ for every vector $x$.
definition: A real [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix), or more generally a complex Hermitian [matrix](c:matrix), $A$ is positive semidefinite if the [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) $x\mapsto x^*Ax$ is never negative. Equivalently, all [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of $A$ are $\ge0$, and equivalently $A=B^*B$ for some matrix $B$.
examples: The identity matrix and every diagonal matrix with entries $\ge0$.
Every matrix $B^TB$ with $B$ real, because $x^TB^TBx=\|Bx\|^2\ge0$.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ is positive semidefinite but not positive definite: its eigenvalues are $2$ and $0$.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$, and $x=(1,-1)$ gives $x^TAx=-2$.

steps: Take a [positive-definite matrix](c:positive-definite-matrix) $A$, so $x^*Ax>0$ for every $x\ne0$.
For $x\ne0$ the value is positive, hence $\ge0$.
For $x=0$ the value is $0$, so $A$ is positive semidefinite.
links.why: It shows that positive semidefinite allows zero values, and positive definite does not.

steps: Take a [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix) $A$.
Look at the quadratic form $x\mapsto x^TAx$.
Add the condition that this form is never negative.
links.why: It shows that positive semidefinite is a sign condition on the quadratic form of a symmetric matrix.

reminder: A principal ideal domain is an integral domain in which every ideal has one generator.
definition: A principal ideal domain (PID) is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$ in which every [ideal](c:ideal) is [principal](c:principal-ideal), that is, equal to $(a)=aR$ for one element $a$.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ are a PID, because every ideal has the form $n\mathbb{Z}$.
The polynomial ring $k[x]$ over a field $k$ is a PID.
Every field is a PID, because its only ideals are $0$ and the whole field.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is an integral domain, but the ideal $(2,x)$ has no single generator.

steps: Take an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$.
Add the condition that every ideal of $R$ is generated by one element.
An integral domain with this condition is a PID.
links.why: It shows that a PID is an integral domain with one extra condition on its ideals.

steps: Take a nonzero ideal $I$ of a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain) and choose a nonzero $a\in I$ of smallest norm.
For $b\in I$ write $b=qa+r$ with $r=0$ or $r$ of smaller norm.
Since $r=b-qa$ lies in $I$, minimality of $a$ forces $r=0$.
So $I=(a)$, and the Euclidean domain is a PID.
links.why: It shows why division with remainder gives principal ideals.

steps: Take a PID $R$. The union of an ascending chain of ideals is an ideal $(a)$, and $a$ lies in one member of the chain.
So every ascending chain of ideals stops, and every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducible elements.
In a PID every irreducible element generates a maximal ideal, so it is prime.
Prime factors make the factorization unique up to order and units, so $R$ is a [unique factorization domain](c:unique-factorization-domain).
links.why: It shows that every PID has unique factorization, as the integers do.

reminder: A quaternion is a number $a+bi+cj+dk$ with real $a,b,c,d$ and $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$.
definition: A quaternion is an element $a+bi+cj+dk$ with [real](c:real-number) coefficients $a,b,c,d$. Quaternions add term by term and multiply by the rules $i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1$. They form a [division ring](c:division-ring) of dimension $4$ over $\mathbb{R}$ that is not commutative, because $ij=-ji$.
examples: Every real number $a$ is the quaternion $a+0i+0j+0k$, and $ij=k$ but $ji=-k$.
A nonzero quaternion $q=a+bi+cj+dk$ has the inverse $\bar q/(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)$, where $\bar q=a-bi-cj-dk$.
Non-example: the algebra of real $2\times2$ matrices has dimension $4$ over $\mathbb{R}$, but it is not the quaternions, because it has nonzero elements without inverse.

steps: Take the quaternions as a real vector space with basis $1,i,j,k$.
The multiplication is bilinear and associative, with unit $1$.
Every nonzero $q$ has the inverse $\bar q/|q|^2$.
So the quaternions are a [division algebra](c:division-algebra) of dimension $4$ over $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: It shows that the quaternions are a real division algebra, and the only noncommutative one of dimension at most $4$.

steps: Take a [complex number](c:complex-number) $a+bi$.
Write it as the quaternion $a+bi+0j+0k$.
Sums and products of such quaternions follow the rules for complex numbers, because $i^2=-1$.
So the complex numbers are a subfield of the quaternions.
links.why: It shows that the quaternions extend the complex numbers and give up commutativity.

reminder: A Radon measure is a Borel measure that is finite on compact sets and regular.
definition: A Radon measure on a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) $X$ is a [Borel measure](c:borel-measure) $\mu$ with $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every [compact](c:compact-space) set $K$. It is also regular: for a [Borel set](c:borel-set) $B$, $\mu(B)$ is the infimum of $\mu(U)$ over open sets $U\supseteq B$, and for an open set $U$, $\mu(U)$ is the supremum of $\mu(K)$ over compact sets $K\subseteq U$. Authors differ in the exact form of regularity.
examples: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a Radon measure.
The Dirac measure $\delta_x$ at a point $x$ of a Hausdorff space is a Radon measure.
Every Haar measure on a locally compact Hausdorff group is a Radon measure.
Non-example: counting measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is a Borel measure, but $\mu([0,1])=\infty$, so it is not finite on compact sets.

steps: Take a [Borel measure](c:borel-measure) $\mu$ on a Hausdorff space.
Add the condition that $\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact set $K$.
Add regularity: Borel sets are approximated from outside by open sets, and open sets from inside by compact sets.
links.why: It shows that a Radon measure is a Borel measure that fits the topology through two conditions.

steps: Take a [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff group $G$.
By definition $\mu$ is a nonzero Borel measure that is regular, finite on compact sets and invariant under left translation.
Forget the invariance and keep the rest.
What remains is a Radon measure on the Hausdorff space $G$.
links.why: It shows that a Haar measure is a Radon measure that is also invariant under the group.

reminder: The Radon-Nikodym derivative $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu$ is the density $f$ with $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ for every set $A$.
definition:
Let $\mu$ and $
u$ be [measures](c:measure) on one [measurable space](c:measurable-space), with $\mu$ $\sigma$-finite and $
u$ [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-measure) with respect to $\mu$. The Radon-Nikodym derivative $\mathrm{d}
u/\mathrm{d}\mu$ is the [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f\ge0$ with $
u(A)=\int_A f\,\mathrm{d}\mu$ for every measurable set $A$. It is unique up to $\mu$-null sets.
examples: If $\mu$ is Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ and $\nu$ is the standard normal law, then $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$.
If $\nu=c\mu$ for a constant $c\ge0$, then $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu=c$.
If $\mu$ is counting measure on a countable set, then $\mathrm{d}\nu/\mathrm{d}\mu(x)=\nu(\{x\})$.
Non-example: the Dirac measure $\delta_0$ has no derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure, because $\delta_0(\{0\})=1$ but $\int_{\{0\}}f\,\mathrm{d}\mu=0$ for every $f$.

steps: Take a probability law $P$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with [density](c:probability-density-function) $p$ with respect to Lebesgue measure $\lambda$.
Then $P(A)=\int_A p\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$ for every Borel set $A$.
This is the defining equation, so $p=\mathrm{d}P/\mathrm{d}\lambda$ is a Radon-Nikodym derivative.
A general reference measure $\mu$ takes the place of $\lambda$.
links.why: It shows that a density is a Radon-Nikodym derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure.

reminder: The rank of a matrix is the largest number of linearly independent columns.
definition: The rank of an $m\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ is the [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-vector-space) of the [span](c:span) of its columns. Equivalently, it is the largest number of [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) columns, and it equals the largest number of linearly independent rows.
examples: The $n\times n$ identity matrix has rank $n$.
The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, because its second column is twice its first column.
The zero matrix has rank $0$.
Non-example: the number of nonzero entries is not the rank, because $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ has four nonzero entries and rank $1$.

reminder: A reflection in a hyperplane sends each point to its mirror image across that hyperplane.
definition: Let $H$ be a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) of [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space). The reflection in $H$ sends a point $x$ to the point $x'$ such that the segment $xx'$ is [perpendicular](c:perpendicular) to $H$ and $H$ cuts it in the middle, so $x$ and $x'$ have the same [distance](c:distance) to $H$ on opposite sides. For $H=\{y:\langle y,n\rangle=0\}$ with unit normal $n$, the formula is $x\mapsto x-2\langle x,n\rangle n$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the reflection in the $x$-axis is $(x,y)\mapsto(x,-y)$.
In $\mathbb{R}^3$ the reflection in the plane $z=0$ is $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,-z)$.
In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the reflection in the line $y=x$ swaps the two coordinates.
Non-example: the rotation $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$ of the plane fixes only the origin, so it is not a reflection in a line.

steps: Write a point as $x=p+tn$ with $p$ in $H$ and $n$ a unit normal.
The reflection $s$ sends $x$ to $p-tn$.
For two points the difference splits the same way, and only the normal part changes sign.
The two parts are orthogonal, so $|s(x)-s(y)|=|x-y|$ and $s$ is an [isometry](c:isometry).
links.why: It shows that a reflection preserves distances, so it belongs to the orthogonal maps of space.

reminder: A regular language is a set of words that a finite automaton accepts.
definition: A [language](c:language) $L$ of finite words over a [finite](c:finite-set) alphabet $\Sigma$ is regular if some [finite automaton](c:finite-automaton) accepts exactly the words of $L$. Equivalently, $L$ is described by a regular expression, built from letters with union, concatenation and star.
examples: The words over $\{a,b\}$ that end in $a$ form a regular language.
The language $(ab)^*=\{\varepsilon,ab,abab,\dots\}$ is regular.
Every finite language is regular.
Non-example: $\{a^nb^n:n\ge0\}$ is not regular, because an automaton with $k$ states cannot count more than $k$ letters $a$.

steps: Take a [language](c:language) $L$, that is, a set of words over a finite alphabet.
Add the condition that some finite automaton accepts exactly the words of $L$.
This condition is strict: there are uncountably many languages and only countably many automata.
links.why: It shows that regular languages are a small class inside all languages.

steps: Take a deterministic finite automaton that accepts $L$.
Make a grammar with one nonterminal $Q$ for each state $q$, and the start state as start symbol.
For each transition $q\xrightarrow{a}r$ add the rule $Q\to aR$, and for each accepting state $q$ add $Q\to\varepsilon$.
This grammar generates exactly $L$ and its rules are context-free, so $L$ is a [context-free language](c:context-free-language).
links.why: It shows that every regular language is context-free, so grammars are at least as strong as automata.

reminder: A regular polygon has all sides equal and all angles equal.
definition: A regular polygon is a [polygon](c:polygon) in which all sides have the same length and all interior [angles](c:angle) are equal.
examples: The equilateral triangle, the square and the regular hexagon are regular polygons.
A regular $n$-gon has all interior angles equal to $(n-2)\cdot180^\circ/n$.
Non-example: a rhombus that is not a square has equal sides but unequal angles, and a rectangle that is not a square has equal angles but unequal sides.

steps: Take a [polygon](c:polygon) with $n$ sides.
Add the condition that all sides have the same length.
Add the condition that all interior angles are equal.
links.why: It shows that a regular polygon is a polygon with two symmetry conditions, one on sides and one on angles.

steps: Take a [square](c:square), which is a polygon with $n=4$ sides.
Its four sides have the same length.
Its four angles are right angles, so they are equal.
So a square is a regular polygon with four sides.
links.why: It shows that the square is the regular polygon with four sides.

reminder: Each element of a regular sequence is a non-zero-divisor on the quotient by the earlier elements.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) and $M$ an $R$-[module](c:module). A sequence $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in $R$ is $M$-regular if each $x_i$ is not a [zero-divisor](c:zero-divisor) on $M/(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1})M$, and $M/(x_1,\dots,x_n)M\ne0$.
examples: The variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ form a regular sequence on the polynomial ring $k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ over a field $k$.
A prime number $p$ is a regular sequence of length one on $\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: $x,xy$ is not a regular sequence in $k[x,y]$, because $xy$ acts as $0$ on $k[x,y]/(x)=k[y]$.

reminder: A regular surface is a subset of space that is covered by smooth parametrized patches with injective differential.
definition: A regular surface is a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^3$ such that every point of $S$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ in $S$ and a [smooth](c:smooth-function) map $x:U\to\mathbb{R}^3$ from an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. The map $x$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) onto $V$ and an [immersion](c:immersion), that is, its [differential](c:differential) $dx_q$ is injective at every $q\in U$.
examples: The unit sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2=1$ is a regular surface.
The graph $z=f(x,y)$ of a smooth function $f$ is a regular surface, with the parametrization $(u,v)\mapsto(u,v,f(u,v))$.
Non-example: the double cone $x^2+y^2=z^2$ is not a regular surface, because a small neighbourhood of the vertex minus the vertex has two pieces, while a plane disc minus a point has one.

steps: Take a regular surface $S$ and a local parametrization $x:U\to V\subseteq S$.
Its inverse $x^{-1}:V\to U$ is a chart onto an open set of $\mathbb{R}^2$.
These charts cover $S$, and the changes of chart are smooth.
So $S$ is a $2$-dimensional [submanifold](c:submanifold) of $\mathbb{R}^3$.
links.why: It shows that a regular surface is a manifold of dimension $2$ inside $\mathbb{R}^3$.

reminder: A point $y$ is a regular value of $f$ if $df_x$ is onto at every point $x$ of $f^{-1}(y)$.
definition: Let $f:M\to N$ be a [smooth](c:smooth-function) map of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold). A point $y\in N$ is a regular value of $f$ if the [differential](c:differential) $df_x:T_xM\to T_yN$ is surjective for every $x$ in the [preimage](c:preimage) $f^{-1}(y)$. Equivalently, $y$ is not the image of a [critical point](c:critical-point) of $f$.
examples: For $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, every $c>0$ is a regular value, and the preimage is a circle.
Every point $y$ outside the image of $f$ is a regular value, because the condition is empty.
For $f(x)=x^3-3x$ on $\mathbb{R}$, every value is regular except $2$ and $-2$.
Non-example: $0$ is not a regular value of $f(x,y)=x^2+y^2$, because $df_{(0,0)}=0$ is not onto $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Take a smooth map $f:M\to N$ and the point $\{y\}$ as a submanifold of $N$ of dimension $0$.
The tangent space of $\{y\}$ is $0$.
So $f$ is transverse to $\{y\}$ exactly when $df_x$ is onto for every $x\in f^{-1}(y)$.
That is the condition that $y$ is a regular value.
links.why: It shows that a regular value is transversality to a single point.

reminder: A relation from $A$ to $B$ is a subset of the Cartesian product $A\times B$.
definition: A binary relation from a [set](c:set) $A$ to a set $B$ is a [subset](c:subset) $R$ of the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $A\times B$. We write $a\,R\,b$ when $(a,b)\in R$, and we say that $a$ is related to $b$.
examples: The order $\le$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is the relation $\{(a,b):a\le b\}$ in $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$.
The divisibility relation on $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of pairs $(a,b)$ with $a\mid b$.
The graph $\{(x,f(x))\}$ of a function $f:A\to B$ is a relation from $A$ to $B$.
Non-example: the condition $a+b=c$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{N}^3$, so it is a ternary relation, not a binary relation.

steps: Take a [function](c:function) $f:A\to B$.
Form its graph $\{(a,f(a)):a\in A\}\subseteq A\times B$.
The graph is a relation from $A$ to $B$.
It relates each $a$ to exactly one $b$, and this condition singles out the functions.
links.why: It shows that a function is a relation in which every input has exactly one output.

steps: Take an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation) $\sim$ on a set $A$.
Its pairs $\{(a,b):a\sim b\}$ form a subset of $A\times A$, so $\sim$ is a relation.
The extra conditions are reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity.
links.why: It shows that an equivalence relation is a relation with three closure conditions.

reminder: The residue of $f$ at $\zeta$ is the coefficient of $(z-\zeta)^{-1}$ in the Laurent series of $f$ at $\zeta$.
definition: Let $f$ be a [meromorphic function](c:meromorphic-function) with the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) $f(z)=\sum_n a_n(z-\zeta)^n$ near a point $\zeta$. The residue of $f$ at $\zeta$ is the coefficient $a_{-1}$. It equals $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint f\,dz$ over a small circle around $\zeta$, so it is what a [contour integral](c:contour-integral) picks up.
examples: The function $1/z$ has residue $1$ at $0$.
The function $1/(z(z-1))$ has residue $-1$ at $0$ and residue $1$ at $1$.
At a simple [pole](c:pole) $\zeta$ the residue is $\lim_{z\to\zeta}(z-\zeta)f(z)$.
Non-example: $1/z^2$ has a pole at $0$ but its residue is $0$, because its Laurent series has no $z^{-1}$ term.

reminder: A topological space is second-countable when its topology has a countable base.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is second-countable if it has a base that is a [countable](c:countable-set) family of [open sets](c:open-set). That is, every open set of $X$ is a union of members of this family.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is second-countable: take the open balls with rational centres and rational radii.
Every countable discrete space is second-countable, with the singletons as base.
Every subspace of a second-countable space is second-countable.
Non-example: an uncountable discrete space is not second-countable, because every base must contain each singleton.

steps: Take a countable base $\mathcal{B}$ of $X$ and a point $x$.
The members of $\mathcal{B}$ that contain $x$ form a countable family.
Every open set around $x$ is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$, so it contains a member that contains $x$.
So this family is a countable neighbourhood base at $x$, and $X$ is [first-countable](c:first-countable-space).
links.why: It shows that a countable base for the whole space gives a countable base at each point.

steps: Take a countable base $\mathcal{B}$ of $X$ and pick one point in each nonempty member.
The chosen points form a countable set $D$.
Every nonempty open set contains a nonempty member of $\mathcal{B}$, so it contains a point of $D$.
So $D$ is dense and $X$ is [separable](c:separable-space).
links.why: It shows that a countable base is a stronger condition than a countable dense subset.

reminder: A separable space has a countable dense subset.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is separable if it has a [countable](c:countable-set) subset $D$ that is [dense](c:dense-subspace), that is, every nonempty open set of $X$ meets $D$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ is separable, with the countable dense subset $\mathbb{Q}^n$.
The Hilbert space $\ell^2$ is separable: the finite sequences with rational entries are dense.
The space $C[0,1]$ with the supremum norm is separable: the polynomials with rational coefficients are dense.
Non-example: the space $\ell^\infty$ of bounded sequences with the supremum norm is not separable, because the uncountably many $0$-$1$ sequences have distance $1$ from each other.

steps: Take a [second-countable](c:second-countable-space) space $X$ with a countable base $\mathcal{B}$.
Choose one point in each nonempty member of $\mathcal{B}$.
The chosen points form a countable set that meets every nonempty open set.
So $X$ is separable.
links.why: It shows that separability is the weaker of the two countability conditions.

steps: A [separable Banach space](c:separable-banach-space) is a Banach space $E$ with a countable subset that is dense for the norm.
The norm gives the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ and so a topology on $E$.
Dense for the norm means dense in this topology.
So $E$ is a separable topological space.
links.why: It shows that separable Banach spaces are the separable spaces that carry a complete norm.

reminder: Two triangles are similar when their corresponding angles are equal.
definition: Two [triangles](c:triangle) are similar if their corresponding [angles](c:angle) are equal. Then the corresponding sides are proportional: there is a number $k>0$ such that each side of the second triangle is $k$ times the matching side of the first.
examples: The triangle with sides $3,4,5$ and the triangle with sides $6,8,10$ are similar, with $k=2$.
Any two equilateral triangles are similar, because all their angles are $60^\circ$.
If a line parallel to $BC$ meets $AB$ and $AC$ at $B'$ and $C'$, then the triangles $AB'C'$ and $ABC$ are similar.
Non-example: the triangles with sides $3,4,5$ and $2,3,4$ are not similar, because the ratios $3/2$, $4/3$ and $5/4$ differ.

reminder: A simplicial object in a category is a contravariant functor from the simplex category into it.
definition: A simplicial object in a [category](c:category) $C$ is a [functor](c:functor) $X:\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to C$, where $\Delta$ is the [simplex category](c:simplex-category) of the finite ordered sets $[n]=\{0<1<\dots<n\}$. It gives objects $X_n$ with face maps $d_i:X_n\to X_{n-1}$ and degeneracy maps $s_i:X_n\to X_{n+1}$ that satisfy the simplicial identities.
examples: A simplicial set is a simplicial object in the category of sets.
A simplicial abelian group is a simplicial object in the category of abelian groups.
The nerve of a category is a simplicial set: $X_n$ is the set of chains of $n$ composable morphisms.
Non-example: a covariant functor $\Delta\to C$ is a cosimplicial object, whose coface maps go from $X_{n-1}$ to $X_n$, not the other way.

steps: Take the category of sets as $C$.
A functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a simplicial object in $\mathbf{Set}$.
Its sets $X_n$ and maps $d_i$ and $s_i$ are the $n$-simplices, faces and degeneracies of a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set).
links.why: It shows that a simplicial set is the case of a simplicial object in the category of sets.

steps: Take a [cosimplicial object](c:cosimplicial-object), that is, a functor $Y:\Delta\to C$.
Passing to opposite categories turns $Y$ into a functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to C^{\mathrm{op}}$.
That is a simplicial object in the category $C^{\mathrm{op}}$.
links.why: It shows that a cosimplicial object in $C$ is a simplicial object in the opposite category.

reminder: A simplicial set is a functor from the opposite of the simplex category to the category of sets.
definition: A simplicial set $X$ is a [functor](c:functor) $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ from the [simplex category](c:simplex-category), that is, a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in the category of sets. It consists of sets $X_n$ of $n$-simplices with face maps and degeneracy maps that satisfy the simplicial identities, and it is a combinatorial model of a space.
examples: The standard $n$-simplex $\Delta^n$ is a simplicial set with $(\Delta^n)_m=\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([m],[n])$.
The singular set of a space $Y$ is a simplicial set: $\operatorname{Sing}(Y)_n$ is the set of continuous maps from the standard $n$-simplex to $Y$.
The nerve of a category is a simplicial set.

Non-example: an abstract [simplicial complex](c:simplicial-complex) is not a simplicial set, because it has no degeneracy maps and no order on its vertices; it gives one only after the vertices are ordered.

steps: Take the category of sets as the category $C$.
A functor $\Delta^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is by definition a [simplicial object](c:simplicial-object) in $\mathbf{Set}$.
So every simplicial set is a simplicial object, with $C=\mathbf{Set}$.
links.why: It shows that results for simplicial objects hold for simplicial sets.

steps: Take a [quasi-category](c:quasi-category), which is a simplicial set $X$.
It has the extra property that every inner horn $\Lambda^n_k\to X$ with $0<k<n$ extends to an $n$-simplex.
Forget this filling property and keep only the simplicial set.
links.why: It shows that a quasi-category is a simplicial set with fillers for inner horns.

reminder: A symplectic manifold is a smooth manifold with a closed nondegenerate differential $2$-form.
definition: A symplectic manifold is a pair $(M,\omega)$ of a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and a [differential form](c:differential-form) $\omega$ of degree $2$ that is [closed](c:closed-differential-form), $d\omega=0$, and [nondegenerate](c:nondegenerate-form) at every point. Nondegenerate means that $v\mapsto\omega(v,\cdot)$ is injective on each tangent space.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ with $\omega=\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$ is a symplectic manifold.
The [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle) $T^*Q$ of any manifold $Q$ is symplectic, with the exterior derivative of the tautological $1$-form, up to sign.
Every oriented surface with an area form is symplectic, for example the sphere $S^2$.
Non-example: the sphere $S^3$ has odd dimension, and a skew-symmetric form on an odd-dimensional space is degenerate, so $S^3$ has no symplectic form.

steps: Take a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of even dimension $2n$.
Choose a $2$-form $\omega$ on $M$.
Require that $d\omega=0$ and that $\omega$ is nondegenerate at every point.
links.why: It shows that a symplectic manifold is a smooth manifold with one extra geometric structure.

steps: Take a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $M$ with metric $g$ and complex structure $J$, and set $\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v)$.
The Kähler condition says that $\omega$ is closed.
The form $\omega$ is nondegenerate, because $g$ is nondegenerate and $J$ is invertible.
So $(M,\omega)$ is a symplectic manifold.
links.why: It shows that every Kähler manifold is symplectic.

reminder: The Taylor series of $f$ at $a$ is the power series with the coefficients $f^{(n)}(a)/n!$.
definition: Let $f$ be infinitely differentiable at a point $a$. Its Taylor series at $a$ is the [power series](c:power-series) $\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n$, built from the [derivatives](c:derivative) of $f$ at $a$ and the [factorials](c:factorial) $n!$. The series may or may not converge to $f$ near $a$.
examples: The Taylor series of $e^x$ at $0$ is $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$.
The Taylor series of $\sin x$ at $0$ is $x-x^3/3!+x^5/5!-\cdots$.
The Taylor series of $1/(1-x)$ at $0$ is the geometric series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$.
Non-example: the Taylor series of $f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ with $f(0)=0$ is $0$, because all derivatives vanish at $0$, so it does not equal $f(x)$ for $x\ne0$.

steps: Take the numbers $a_n=f^{(n)}(a)/n!$.
Form the series $\sum_n a_n(x-a)^n$.
This is a [power series](c:power-series) centred at $a$.
So a Taylor series is a power series whose coefficients come from the derivatives of $f$.
links.why: It shows that a Taylor series is a power series with a fixed rule for its coefficients.

steps: Take $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$ and $a=0$.
The derivatives satisfy $f^{(n)}(0)=(-1)^{n-1}(n-1)!$ for $n\ge1$.
Divide by $n!$ to get the coefficients $(-1)^{n-1}/n$.
So the Taylor series is $x-x^2/2+x^3/3-\cdots$, the [Mercator series](c:mercator-series).
links.why: It shows that the Mercator series is the Taylor series of the logarithm.

reminder: A topological group is a group whose multiplication and inversion are continuous.
definition: A topological group is a [group](c:group) $G$ with a [topology](c:topological-space) such that the multiplication $G\times G\to G$ and the inversion $G\to G$ are [continuous](c:continuous-function). The product $G\times G$ carries the product topology.
examples: The real numbers $(\mathbb{R},+)$ and the circle group $S^1$ are topological groups.
The group $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ with the subspace topology from $\mathbb{R}^{n^2}$ is a topological group.
Every group with the discrete topology is a topological group.
Non-example: the Sorgenfrey line, with basic open sets $[a,b)$, is not a topological group under addition, because inversion $x\mapsto-x$ sends $[a,b)$ to $(-b,-a]$, which is not open.

steps: Work in the category of topological spaces, which has finite products.
A [group object](c:group-object) there is a space $G$ with continuous maps for multiplication, unit and inversion.
These maps satisfy the group laws as equalities of continuous maps.
That is exactly a topological group.
links.why: It shows that a topological group is a group object in the category of spaces.

steps: Take a [Lie group](c:lie-group): a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inversion.
Smooth maps are continuous, so both maps are continuous.
A manifold is a topological space.
So a Lie group is a topological group.
links.why: It shows that a Lie group is a topological group with a smooth structure.

steps: Take any group $G$ and give it the discrete topology.
Every subset of $G\times G$ is open, so every map out of $G\times G$ is continuous.
Every subset of $G$ is open, so inversion is continuous too.
So $G$ is a topological group.
links.why: It shows that every abstract group is a topological group with the discrete topology.

reminder: The group $K(X)$ is the group completion of the monoid of isomorphism classes of vector bundles over $X$.
definition: For a [compact](c:compact-space) Hausdorff space $X$, the group $K(X)$ is the [Grothendieck group](c:grothendieck-group) of the monoid of isomorphism classes of complex [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) over $X$ under direct sum. Extending $K$ to the groups $K^{-n}$ by suspension gives a generalized [cohomology](c:cohomology) theory, which Bott periodicity makes $2$-periodic.
examples: $K(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{Z}$, and the class of a bundle is its rank.
$K(S^2)\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}$, generated by the trivial line bundle and the Hopf line bundle.
$K(S^1)\cong\mathbb{Z}$, because every vector bundle on the circle is trivial.
Non-example: the set of isomorphism classes of vector bundles over $X$ is not $K(X)$, because it is only a monoid under direct sum and has no inverses until we take the group completion.

steps: Take the trivial group $G=\{e\}$.
A $G$-equivariant vector bundle over $X$ is just a vector bundle over $X$.
So the group $K_G(X)$ of [equivariant K-theory](c:equivariant-k-theory) equals $K(X)$.
links.why: It shows that topological K-theory is equivariant K-theory with the trivial group acting.

steps: Take the trivial twist, the zero class in $H^3(X;\mathbb{Z})$.
For this twist the twisted bundles are ordinary vector bundles.
So [twisted K-theory](c:twisted-k-theory) with the trivial twist is $K(X)$.
links.why: It shows that topological K-theory is twisted K-theory with the zero twist.

reminder: A topological vector space is a vector space whose addition and scalar multiplication are continuous.
definition: A topological vector space is a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with a [topology](c:topological-space) for which addition $V\times V\to V$ and scalar multiplication $\mathbb{K}\times V\to V$ are [continuous](c:continuous-function). Many authors also ask that points are closed.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ with its usual topology is a topological vector space.
Every normed space is one, for example $C[0,1]$ with the supremum norm.
The product $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ with the product topology is one whose topology comes from no norm.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ as a real vector space with the discrete topology is not one, because $t\mapsto t\cdot1$ from the usual $\mathbb{R}$ to the discrete $\mathbb{R}$ is not continuous.

steps: Take a [normed space](c:normed-space) $E$ with the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ and its topology.
Addition is continuous, because $\|(x+y)-(x'+y')\|\le\|x-x'\|+\|y-y'\|$.
Scalar multiplication is continuous, because $\|\lambda x-\lambda'x'\|\le|\lambda|\|x-x'\|+|\lambda-\lambda'|\|x'\|$.
So $E$ is a topological vector space.
links.why: It shows that every norm gives a topological vector space, and that the converse fails.

steps: Take a [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) $V$, a vector space with a topology that has convex neighbourhoods of $0$ as a base.
Forget that the neighbourhoods are convex, and keep the vector space and the topology.
Addition and scalar multiplication stay continuous, so $V$ is a topological vector space.
links.why: It shows that local convexity is the extra condition that gives Hahn-Banach style separation.

reminder: The total degree of a polynomial is the largest sum of exponents among its monomials.
definition: Let $f$ be a nonzero [polynomial](c:polynomial) in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$. The total degree of $f$ is the maximum of $e_1+\dots+e_n$ over all [monomials](c:monomial) $x_1^{e_1}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ that occur in $f$ with a nonzero coefficient.
examples: The polynomial $x^2y+z$ has total degree $3$.
The polynomial $x^3y-xy+5$ has monomials of degree $4$, $2$ and $0$, so its total degree is $4$.
A nonzero constant has total degree $0$.
Non-example: the degree of $x^2y^5$ in $x$ alone is $2$, but its total degree is $7$.

steps: Take a polynomial $f$ in one variable $x$.
Each monomial $x^k$ has exponent sum $k$.
So the largest exponent sum is the largest $k$ that occurs, which is the usual [degree](c:degree-of-a-polynomial) of $f$.
links.why: It shows that total degree is the usual degree when there is only one variable.

reminder: Two submanifolds are transverse when, at each common point, their tangent spaces together span the ambient tangent space.
definition: Let $f:M\to N$ be a [smooth](c:smooth-function) map of [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) and $Z\subseteq N$ a [submanifold](c:submanifold). The map $f$ is transverse to $Z$, written $f\pitchfork Z$, if $df_x(T_xM)+T_{f(x)}Z=T_{f(x)}N$ for every $x$ with $f(x)\in Z$. Two submanifolds are transverse if the inclusion of one is transverse to the other, that is, if $T_pA+T_pB=T_pN$ at each common point $p$.
examples: The $x$-axis and the $y$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^2$ are transverse, because their tangent lines span $\mathbb{R}^2$.
A line that meets a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ in one point is transverse to it, because $1+2=3$ dimensions span.
If $y$ is a regular value of $f$, then $f$ is transverse to the point $\{y\}$.
Non-example: the parabola $y=x^2$ and the $x$-axis meet at the origin with the same tangent line, which spans only a line of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

steps: Take a smooth map $f:M\to N$ and the point $\{y\}$ as a submanifold of $N$.
Its tangent space is $0$, so $f\pitchfork\{y\}$ means that $df_x$ is onto for every $x\in f^{-1}(y)$.
That is exactly the condition that $y$ is a [regular value](c:regular-value) of $f$.
links.why: It shows that regular values are the case of transversality to a single point.

reminder: A Turing machine reads and writes symbols on an unbounded tape by a finite table of state rules.
definition: A Turing machine has a [finite](c:finite-set) set $Q$ of states, a finite alphabet $\Gamma$ with a blank symbol, and an infinite tape of cells that each hold one symbol. A transition [function](c:function) $\delta:Q\times\Gamma\to Q\times\Gamma\times\{L,R\}$ tells the head, from the current state and the symbol it reads, which symbol to write, which way to move and which state to enter. The machine halts when no rule applies.
examples: A machine that adds $1$ to a binary number: it goes to the right end, then turns trailing $1$s into $0$s, and writes $1$ on the first $0$ or blank.
A machine that decides if a word is a palindrome by comparing the first and the last symbol and erasing them.
A universal Turing machine reads the description of another machine and simulates it.
Non-example: a machine with a tape of fixed finite length has only finitely many configurations, so it is a finite automaton, not a Turing machine.

steps: Take a deterministic [finite automaton](c:finite-automaton).
Make a Turing machine with the same states, that reads the input from left to right.
It writes back each symbol that it reads, and it always moves right.
It accepts when it reads the blank after the input in an accepting state.
links.why: It shows that a finite automaton is a Turing machine that never writes and never moves left.

reminder: The unit disc is the set of complex numbers $z$ with $|z|<1$.
definition: The open unit disc is the set $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ of [complex numbers](c:complex-number) at distance less than $1$ from $0$. Its boundary is the unit [circle](c:circle), the set $|z|=1$, which is not part of it.
examples: The numbers $0$ and $\tfrac12+\tfrac{i}{3}$ lie in $\mathbb{D}$.
The points $re^{i\theta}$ with $0\le r<1$ fill $\mathbb{D}$.
The geometric series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n$ converges exactly on $\mathbb{D}$.
Non-example: the numbers $1$ and $i$ have $|z|=1$, so they lie on the unit circle and not in the open unit disc.

steps: Identify $\mathbb{C}$ with the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and use the metric $d(z,w)=|z-w|$.
The open [ball](c:ball) of radius $1$ around $0$ is $\{z:|z-0|<1\}$.
This set is exactly $\mathbb{D}$.
links.why: It shows that the unit disc is the open ball of radius $1$ in the complex plane.

reminder: A univalent function is a holomorphic function that is injective on its domain.
definition: A univalent function is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f:U\to\mathbb{C}$ on a domain $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ that is an [injection](c:injection). Usually $U$ is the [unit disc](c:unit-disc) and $f$ is normalized by $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$.
examples: The identity $f(z)=z$ is univalent on the unit disc.
The Koebe function $f(z)=z/(1-z)^2$ is univalent on the unit disc, and it maps the disc onto the plane minus the slit $(-\infty,-1/4]$.
The map $z\mapsto(z-a)/(1-\bar az)$ with $|a|<1$ is univalent on the unit disc.
Non-example: $f(z)=z^2$ is not univalent on the unit disc, because $f(\tfrac12)=f(-\tfrac12)$.

steps: Take a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ on a domain $U$.
Add the condition that $f$ is injective on $U$.
A holomorphic function with this condition is univalent.
links.why: It shows that univalent is holomorphic plus injective, and that the Koebe-type theorems limit how such maps can grow.

steps: Take a univalent function $f$ on $U$.
An injective holomorphic function has $f'(z)\ne0$ at every point of $U$.
A holomorphic function with $f'(z)\ne0$ preserves angles and orientation at $z$.
So $f$ is a [conformal map](c:conformal-map) from $U$ onto the open set $f(U)$.
links.why: It shows that a univalent function is a conformal map that is also one-to-one.

reminder: The winding number counts how many times a closed curve goes around a point.
definition: For a closed [continuous](c:continuous-function) curve $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{C}$ and a point $p$ not on it, the winding number $n(\gamma,p)$ is the [integer](c:integer) that is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-continuous-function) of the map $t\mapsto(\gamma(t)-p)/|\gamma(t)-p|$ from the [circle](c:circle) to itself. Equivalently, it is the class of $\gamma$ in the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(\mathbb{C}\setminus\{p\})\cong\mathbb{Z}$, and for a piecewise smooth curve it equals $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\gamma\frac{dz}{z-p}$.
examples: The circle $t\mapsto e^{it}$ with $0\le t\le2\pi$ has winding number $1$ around $0$.
The curve $t\mapsto e^{-2it}$ with $0\le t\le2\pi$ has winding number $-2$ around $0$: it goes twice around, clockwise.
The unit circle has winding number $0$ around the point $2$, because it does not enclose that point.
Non-example: the path $t\mapsto e^{it}$ with $0\le t\le\pi$ is not closed and has no winding number, because its angle changes by $\pi$, not by a multiple of $2\pi$.

steps: Take a closed curve $\gamma$ and a point $p$ not on it.
The map $u(t)=(\gamma(t)-p)/|\gamma(t)-p|$ is a continuous map from the circle to the circle.
The [degree](c:degree-of-a-continuous-function) of $u$ is the number of times that $u$ wraps around the circle.
This degree is the winding number $n(\gamma,p)$.
links.why: It shows that a winding number is the degree of a map from the circle to the circle.

reminder: A $4$-manifold is a space that looks locally like $\mathbb{R}^4$ at every point.
definition: A $4$-manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) of [dimension](c:dimension-of-a-manifold) $4$: a Hausdorff, second-countable space in which every point has a neighbourhood [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism) to an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^4$. In the smooth case the changes of chart are smooth.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^4$ and the [4-sphere](c:4-sphere) $S^4$ are $4$-manifolds.
The [complex projective plane](c:complex-projective-plane) $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is a closed $4$-manifold.
The product $S^2\times S^2$ and the torus $T^4$ are closed $4$-manifolds.
Non-example: the $3$-sphere $S^3$ has dimension $3$, so it is not a $4$-manifold.

steps: Take a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$.
Require that every point has a chart onto an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n=4$.
Then $M$ is a $4$-manifold.
links.why: It shows that a $4$-manifold is a manifold whose dimension is fixed at $4$.

steps: Take $\mathbb{CP}^2$, the space of complex lines in $\mathbb{C}^3$.
Its standard charts $\{z_i\ne0\}$ are homeomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^2\cong\mathbb{R}^4$.
The space is Hausdorff and second-countable, and the charts cover it.
So $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is a $4$-manifold.
links.why: It shows that the complex projective plane is a basic example of a closed $4$-manifold.

reminder: An antiunitary operator is an antilinear bijection of a Hilbert space that preserves inner products up to complex conjugation.
definition: An antiunitary operator on a complex [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\mathscr{H}$ is a bijective [antilinear map](c:antilinear-map) $\Theta:\mathscr{H}\to\mathscr{H}$ with $\langle\Theta x,\Theta y\rangle=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle}$ for all $x,y$, where the bar is [complex conjugation](c:complex-conjugation). Antilinear means $\Theta(\lambda x+\mu y)=\bar\lambda\,\Theta x+\bar\mu\,\Theta y$.
examples: Complex conjugation $(z_1,\dots,z_n)\mapsto(\bar z_1,\dots,\bar z_n)$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ is antiunitary.
The time-reversal operator $\Theta=i\sigma_yK$ of a spin-$\tfrac12$ particle is antiunitary, where $K$ is complex conjugation.
Non-example: a unitary operator $U$ is linear and has $\langle Ux,Uy\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$ without a conjugate, so it is not antiunitary.

steps: Take an antiunitary operator $\Theta$. It is additive, so $\Theta x-\Theta y=\Theta(x-y)$.
For every $z$, $\|\Theta z\|^2=\langle\Theta z,\Theta z\rangle=\overline{\langle z,z\rangle}=\|z\|^2$.
Hence $\|\Theta x-\Theta y\|=\|x-y\|$, so $\Theta$ preserves distances.
It is also bijective, so it is an [isometry](c:isometry) of $\mathscr{H}$ onto itself.
links.why: It shows that an antiunitary operator is a distance-preserving map even though it is not linear.

reminder: A Borel subgroup is a maximal closed connected solvable subgroup of a linear algebraic group.
definition: Let $G$ be a [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group). A Borel subgroup of $G$ is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $B$ that is closed in the [Zariski topology](c:zariski-topology), connected and [solvable](c:solvable-group), and that is maximal among the subgroups with these three properties.
examples: In $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$ the invertible [upper triangular matrices](c:upper-triangular-matrix) form a Borel subgroup.
In $SL_2(\mathbb{C})$ the upper triangular matrices of determinant $1$ form a Borel subgroup.
If $G$ is connected and solvable, for example a torus, then $G$ is its own Borel subgroup.
Non-example: the diagonal torus of $GL_2(\mathbb{C})$ is closed, connected and solvable, but it lies in the upper triangular group, so it is not maximal.

steps: Take a [subgroup](c:subgroup) $B$ of a linear algebraic group $G$.
Require that $B$ is Zariski closed, connected and solvable.
Require that no larger subgroup of $G$ has these three properties.
links.why: It shows that a Borel subgroup is a subgroup picked out by closedness, connectedness, solvability and maximality.

steps: Take a Borel subgroup $B$ of a connected linear algebraic group $G$.
The quotient $G/B$ is a projective variety, the [flag variety](c:flag-variety).
A closed subgroup $P$ is [parabolic](c:parabolic-subgroup) when $G/P$ is a complete variety.
So $B$ is a parabolic subgroup, and it is the smallest kind.
links.why: It shows that Borel subgroups are the minimal parabolic subgroups.

reminder: A bump function is a smooth function that is not zero everywhere and vanishes outside a compact set.
definition: A bump function is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $\varphi$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, or on a manifold, that is not identically zero and has [compact support](c:compact-support): $\varphi=0$ outside some compact set. Often one also asks that $0\le\varphi\le1$.
examples: The function $\varphi(x)=\exp\!\big(-1/(1-x^2)\big)$ for $|x|<1$ and $\varphi(x)=0$ otherwise is a bump function on $\mathbb{R}$.
The product $\varphi(x_1)\cdots\varphi(x_n)$ is a bump function on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Every translate and rescaling $\varphi((x-a)/r)$ of a bump function is a bump function.
Non-example: the Gaussian $e^{-x^2}$ is smooth but is nonzero everywhere, so its support is not compact, and the tent function $\max(0,1-|x|)$ has compact support but is not smooth.

steps: Take a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Add the condition that $f$ vanishes outside a compact set.
Add the condition that $f$ is not identically zero.
links.why: It shows that a bump function is a smooth function that is localized to a compact region.

reminder: A canonical divisor of a smooth variety is the divisor of a nonzero rational differential form of top degree.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth [algebraic variety](c:algebraic-variety) of dimension $n$. A canonical divisor $K_X$ is the [divisor](c:divisor) $\sum_D\operatorname{ord}_D(\omega)\,D$ of a nonzero rational $n$-form $\omega$ on $X$. Its line bundle is the [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle), and $K_X$ is defined up to linear equivalence.
examples: On $\mathbb{P}^1$ the form $dz$ has no zeros or poles on the affine line and a double pole at infinity, so $K=-2[\infty]$.
On an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) the form $dz$ has no zeros or poles, so $K=0$.
On $\mathbb{P}^n$ one has $K=-(n+1)H$ for a hyperplane class $H$.
Non-example: a hyperplane section $H$ of $\mathbb{P}^2$ is not a canonical divisor, because it has degree $1$ and $K_{\mathbb{P}^2}=-3H$ has degree $-3$.

steps: Take a nonzero rational $n$-form $\omega$ on the smooth variety $X$.
Count the order of vanishing of $\omega$ along each prime [divisor](c:divisor) $D$, and form $\sum_D\operatorname{ord}_D(\omega)D$.
That sum is a divisor, and another choice of $\omega$ changes it by a principal divisor.
links.why: It shows that the canonical divisor is one divisor class that comes from the differential forms of the variety.

reminder: A Cauchy surface is a hypersurface that every inextendible timelike curve meets exactly once.
definition: A Cauchy surface in a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold), which models a [spacetime](c:spacetime), is a [hypersurface](c:hypersurface) $S$ that every inextendible [timelike curve](c:timelike-curve) meets exactly once. It stands for all of space at one moment of time.
examples: In Minkowski spacetime the slice $t=0$ is a Cauchy surface, and so is every slice $t=\text{const}$.
In the Einstein static universe $\mathbb{R}\times S^3$ the slice $\{0\}\times S^3$ is a Cauchy surface.
Non-example: the plane $x=0$ in Minkowski spacetime is not a Cauchy surface, because the timelike curve $x=1$, $y=z=0$ never meets it.

steps: Take a [hypersurface](c:hypersurface) $S$ in a Lorentzian manifold $M$.
Look at an inextendible timelike curve in $M$.
Require that every such curve meets $S$ exactly once.
links.why: It shows that a Cauchy surface is a hypersurface that every observer crosses once.

reminder: The Cayley graph of a group with generators has the group elements as vertices and an edge $g\to gx$ for each generator $x$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $X\subseteq G$ a set of [generators](c:generator). The Cayley graph is the [directed graph](c:directed-graph) with vertex set $G$ and one edge from $g$ to $gx$, labelled $x$, for each $g\in G$ and $x\in X$. Left multiplication by $G$ acts on it by graph automorphisms.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{Z}$ and $X=\{1\}$ the Cayley graph is the line with an edge $n\to n+1$ for each $n$.
For $G=\mathbb{Z}^2$ and $X=\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ the Cayley graph is the square grid.
For the free group on two generators the Cayley graph is a tree in which each vertex has four edges.

Non-example: a path with three vertices is the Cayley graph of no group, because its middle vertex has degree $2$ and its end vertices have degree $1$, while left multiplication makes all vertices look alike.

steps: Take the elements of the group $G$ as vertices.
Join $g$ to $gx$ by an edge labelled $x$, for each $x\in X$.
The result is a labelled [directed graph](c:directed-graph), and $G$ acts on it by left multiplication.
links.why: It shows that a Cayley graph is a directed graph with a free and transitive group action.

steps: A [Schreier graph](c:schreier-graph) has the cosets of a subgroup $H$ as vertices and an edge $Hg\to Hgx$ for each generator $x$.
Take the trivial subgroup $H=\{e\}$.
Then each coset is one element $g$, and the edges are $g\to gx$.
That is the Cayley graph.
links.why: It shows that a Cayley graph is a Schreier graph for the trivial subgroup.

reminder: The Chern character is the ring homomorphism from K-theory to rational cohomology that sends a line bundle $L$ to $e^{c_1(L)}$.
definition: The Chern character is the map $\mathrm{ch}:K(X)\to H^*(X;\mathbb{Q})$ from [topological K-theory](c:topological-k-theory) to rational [cohomology](c:cohomology) with $\mathrm{ch}(E\oplus F)=\mathrm{ch}(E)+\mathrm{ch}(F)$, $\mathrm{ch}(E\otimes F)=\mathrm{ch}(E)\,\mathrm{ch}(F)$ and $\mathrm{ch}(L)=e^{c_1(L)}$ for a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$. For a bundle with Chern roots $x_i$ it is $\mathrm{ch}=\sum_i e^{x_i}$.
examples: The trivial bundle of rank $r$ has $\mathrm{ch}=r$.
On $\mathbb{CP}^1$ the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(1)$ has $\mathrm{ch}=1+h$, where $h$ generates $H^2$ and $h^2=0$.
For a bundle $E$, $\mathrm{ch}(E)=\operatorname{rk}E+c_1(E)+\tfrac12\big(c_1(E)^2-2c_2(E)\big)+\cdots$.
Non-example: the total Chern class $c$ is not a ring homomorphism from $K$-theory, because $c(E\oplus F)=c(E)\,c(F)$ turns sums into products.

steps: Take a vector bundle $E$ over $X$.
Assign the rational class $\mathrm{ch}(E)=\sum_i e^{x_i}$ computed from its Chern roots.
This assignment commutes with pullback: $\mathrm{ch}(f^*E)=f^*\mathrm{ch}(E)$.
So each degree of $\mathrm{ch}$ is a rational [characteristic class](c:characteristic-class).
links.why: It shows that the Chern character packs the characteristic classes of a bundle into one ring homomorphism.

reminder: A chord is a line segment whose two endpoints lie on a circle.
definition: A chord of a [circle](c:circle) is a [line segment](c:line-segment) whose two endpoints lie on the circle. A chord that passes through the centre is a [diameter](c:diameter).
examples: The diameter is the longest chord of a circle.
Every side of a polygon inscribed in a circle is a chord of that circle.
If two chords $AB$ and $CD$ meet at $P$, then $PA\cdot PB=PC\cdot PD$.
Non-example: a radius is not a chord, because one endpoint is the centre, which does not lie on the circle.

steps: Take a circle and two different points $A$ and $B$ on it.
Join them by the [line segment](c:line-segment) $AB$.
This segment, with both endpoints on the circle, is a chord.
links.why: It shows that a chord is a line segment whose endpoints are constrained to a circle.

steps: Take a [diameter](c:diameter) of a circle, a segment through the centre.
Both of its endpoints lie on the circle, so it is a chord.
It is the chord that passes through the centre.
links.why: It shows that a diameter is the longest chord, the one through the centre.

reminder: A clopen subset of a topological space is both open and closed.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $A$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is clopen if it is both [open](c:open-set) and [closed](c:closed-set). Equivalently, $A$ and its [complement](c:complement) are both open.
examples: The empty set and $X$ itself are clopen in every space.
In a discrete space every subset is clopen.
In $X=[0,1]\cup[2,3]\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ the part $[0,1]$ is clopen.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{R}$ the interval $[0,1)$ is neither open nor closed, and $(0,1)$ is open but not closed.

steps: Take an [open set](c:open-set) $A$ of $X$.
Add the condition that $A$ is closed, that is, that $X\setminus A$ is open.
Then $A$ is clopen.
links.why: It shows that a clopen set is an open set whose complement is also open.

steps: Take a [closed set](c:closed-set) $A$ of $X$.
Add the condition that $A$ is open, that is, that $X\setminus A$ is closed.
Then $A$ is clopen.
links.why: It shows that a clopen set is a closed set that is also open.

reminder: Two closed manifolds are cobordant when together they form the boundary of a compact manifold.
definition: Two closed [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and $N$ of dimension $n$ are cobordant if there is a [compact](c:compact-space) smooth $(n+1)$-manifold $W$ whose boundary is the disjoint union $M\sqcup N$. In the oriented version $W$ is oriented and $\partial W=M\sqcup\overline{N}$, where $\overline{N}$ is $N$ with the reverse orientation.
examples: A circle and two disjoint circles are cobordant, because a sphere with three holes has these circles as its boundary.
Every closed manifold $M$ is cobordant to itself, through $M\times[0,1]$ with boundary $M\sqcup M$.
The sphere $S^n$ is cobordant to the empty manifold, because it bounds the disc $D^{n+1}$.
Non-example: in the oriented version, $\mathbb{CP}^2$ is not cobordant to the empty manifold, because its signature is $1$ and the signature of a boundary is $0$.

steps: Take an [h-cobordism](c:h-cobordism): a compact manifold $W$ with $\partial W=M\sqcup N$.
Both inclusions $M\to W$ and $N\to W$ are homotopy equivalences.
Drop the homotopy condition and keep only $\partial W=M\sqcup N$.
So every h-cobordism is a cobordism.
links.why: It shows that an h-cobordism is a cobordism whose ends are homotopy equivalent to the middle.

reminder: A coequalizer of $f,g:A\to B$ is a universal morphism $q:B\to Q$ with $qf=qg$.
definition: Let $f,g:A\to B$ be two parallel morphisms in a [category](c:category). A coequalizer is a morphism $q:B\to Q$ with $qf=qg$ such that every morphism $h:B\to T$ with $hf=hg$ factors as $h=uq$ for exactly one $u:Q\to T$. It is the [colimit](c:colimit) of the diagram $A\rightrightarrows B$.
examples: In sets the coequalizer is the quotient $B/{\sim}$ for the equivalence relation generated by $f(a)\sim g(a)$.
In abelian groups the coequalizer is $B/\operatorname{im}(f-g)$.
In groups the coequalizer is the quotient of $B$ by the normal subgroup generated by all $f(a)g(a)^{-1}$.
Non-example: if $f=g$, the coequalizer is $\mathrm{id}_B$, and the map $B\to0$ in abelian groups has $qf=qg$ but is not universal when $B\ne0$.

steps: Take the category with two objects and two parallel arrows.
A diagram of this shape is the pair $f,g:A\to B$.
A cocone over it is a morphism $q:B\to Q$ with $qf=qg$.
The [colimit](c:colimit) is the universal cocone, which is the coequalizer.
links.why: It shows that a coequalizer is the colimit of a parallel pair.

steps: Take an [absolute coequalizer](c:absolute-coequalizer) $q:B\to Q$ of $f$ and $g$.
By definition $qf=qg$ and $q$ is universal for this property.
Its extra property is that every functor sends it to a coequalizer.
So it is a coequalizer with an added preservation property.
links.why: It shows that an absolute coequalizer is a coequalizer that every functor preserves.

reminder: A compact Lie group is a Lie group whose underlying manifold is compact.
definition: A compact Lie group is a [Lie group](c:lie-group) whose underlying manifold is a [compact space](c:compact-space). Every compact Lie group is isomorphic to a closed subgroup of some unitary group $U(n)$.
examples: The circle group $S^1=U(1)$ is a compact Lie group.
The groups $SO(n)$, $U(n)$ and $SU(2)\cong S^3$ are compact Lie groups.
Every finite group is a compact Lie group of dimension $0$.
Non-example: $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ is a Lie group but is not compact, because its entries can be arbitrarily large, and $(\mathbb{R},+)$ is not compact either.

steps: Take a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$.
Add the condition that its underlying manifold is compact.
Then $G$ is a compact Lie group.
links.why: It shows that a compact Lie group is a Lie group with one finiteness condition.

steps: Take a compact Lie group $G$.
Its multiplication and inversion are smooth, hence continuous, so $G$ is a topological group.
Its underlying space is compact and Hausdorff.
So $G$ is a [compact group](c:compact-group).
links.why: It shows that results for compact groups, such as Haar measure and the Peter-Weyl theorem, apply to compact Lie groups.

reminder: A complete local ring is a local ring that is complete for the topology of its maximal ideal.
definition: A [local ring](c:local-ring) $(R,\mathfrak{m})$ is complete if it is complete in the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology, that is, every Cauchy sequence converges. Equivalently, the natural map from $R$ to its [adic completion](c:adic-completion) $\varprojlim_n R/\mathfrak{m}^n$ is an isomorphism, where $\mathfrak{m}$ is the [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal).
examples: The ring $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of $p$-adic integers is a complete local ring.
The ring $k[[x_1,\dots,x_n]]$ of formal power series over a field $k$ is a complete local ring.
Every field is a complete local ring, with $\mathfrak{m}=0$.
Non-example: $k[x]_{(x)}$ is a local ring but is not complete, because the partial sums of $\sum_n x^{n^2}$ form a Cauchy sequence whose sum is not a rational function.

steps: Take a [local ring](c:local-ring) $(R,\mathfrak{m})$.
Give $R$ the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology.
Add the condition that every Cauchy sequence converges in $R$.
links.why: It shows that completeness is one extra condition on the topology of a local ring.

steps: Take a monic polynomial $f$ over $R$ and an element $a_0$ with $f(a_0)\in\mathfrak{m}$ and $f'(a_0)$ a unit.
The Newton step $a_{n+1}=a_n-f(a_n)/f'(a_n)$ gives $f(a_n)\in\mathfrak{m}^{2^n}$.
So $(a_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence for the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology.
Completeness gives a limit $a$ with $f(a)=0$ that lifts $a_0$, so $R$ is a [Henselian ring](c:henselian-ring).
links.why: It shows that Hensel's lemma holds in every complete local ring.

reminder: A linear map between C*-algebras is completely positive when every matrix amplification of it is positive.
definition: A linear map $\varphi:A_1\to A_2$ between [C*-algebras](c:c-star-algebra) is completely positive if for every $k\ge1$ the amplification $\varphi_k:M_k(A_1)\to M_k(A_2)$, $[a_{ij}]\mapsto[\varphi(a_{ij})]$, sends [positive elements](c:positive-element) to positive elements. Here $M_k(A)$ is the [matrix algebra](c:matrix-algebra) of the $k\times k$ matrices over $A$.
examples: Every $*$-homomorphism between C*-algebras is completely positive.
For a fixed operator $V$, the map $a\mapsto V^*aV$ is completely positive.
Every positive linear functional $\varphi:A\to\mathbb{C}$ on a C*-algebra is completely positive.

Non-example: the transpose map on $M_2(\mathbb{C})$ is positive but not completely positive, because $\varphi_2$ sends the positive matrix $\sum_{i,j}E_{ij}\otimes E_{ij}$ to the swap matrix, which has the eigenvalue $-1$.

steps: Take a completely positive map $\varphi$ and use $k=1$.
Then $\varphi_1=\varphi$ sends positive elements to positive elements.
So $\varphi$ is a [positive linear map](c:positive-linear-map), and the extra condition is the positivity of all amplifications $\varphi_k$.
links.why: It shows that complete positivity is stronger than positivity, as the transpose map shows.

steps: Take a [positive linear functional](c:positive-linear-functional) $\varphi$ on $A$, a positive $a=[a_{ij}]$ in $M_k(A)$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^k$.
The element $\sum_{i,j}\bar\lambda_i a_{ij}\lambda_j$ of $A$ is positive.
So $\langle\lambda,\varphi_k(a)\lambda\rangle=\varphi\big(\sum_{i,j}\bar\lambda_i a_{ij}\lambda_j\big)\ge0$, and $\varphi_k(a)$ is positive.
Hence $\varphi$ is completely positive.
links.why: It shows that every positive functional on a C*-algebra is completely positive.
